item.title: ENB’s Chloe Keneally on the 'beautiful family tradition’ of The Nutcracker
item.dc:creator: Emmie Newitt
item.description:
This Christmas, families will flock to the London Coliseum to enjoy The Nutcracker, a much-loved festive tradition. Although the ballet is performed on stages across the UK during the Christmas season, there is something particularly special about experiencing the magic of this timeless production brought to life by over 100 dancers from the English National Ballet and live musicians. Playing one of the main roles in the show is Chloe Keneally, and she shared with us more about this iconic production.

Having been a member of the English National Ballet since 2019, how does it feel to have worked your way up to soloist and to be able to debut your new role within the company during the iconic ‘Nutcracker’?

I feel incredibly proud to be where I am right now in my career, especially having been recently promoted to soloist with the company. It all still feels surreal performing as Clara on opening night, as I remember coming to watch the dress rehearsal of English National Ballet’s Nutcracker when I first moved to London as a student at ENB School, leaving so inspired and dreaming that one day it would be me on the Coliseum stage performing Clara. So, it really is a full circle moment.  

How have you been preparing for Clara and how has it differed from previous roles you played when you were in the corps de ballet and a first artist?

As Clara, being on stage for most of the show and having to carry the story of a ballet is a newer experience for me, but one that I really love. You feel so much more a part of the story and are fully immersed in the show. As a member of the corps de ballet, you have so much responsibility towards your colleagues, and it gives you a very different sense of fulfilment at the end of the show, but also one that I love and value. 

The Nutcracker's fantastical, nonsensical nature is arguably what makes it a Christmas classic that people return to year after year. As Clara, how have you found that childlike play within the rigidity of classic ballet?

Clara’s world in the Nutcracker is so fun! It’s full of wonder and curiosity, and I think that there is such a sense of freedom in her role as you’re really allowed to react to everything that is happening around you. For me, going back and remembering why I first started dancing, and bringing that sense of joy through the character, makes it feel really authentic.  

Set in the Edwardian era during the Suffragettes Movement, how has the inclusion of Suffragettes within the piece helped not only to drive your own character but to reframe Clara’s journey from a traditional fairytale to one of self-discovery and empowerment?

Arielle and Aaron were really inspired by the Suffragettes Movement when they were creating this production. So the impact these women had on Clara’s story was quite significant. I think when Clara encounters the Suffragettes early on in the ballet, she is inspired by them for their courage and commitment to their beliefs. Clara is really in control of driving her own narrative and is confident enough in herself to be a bold young woman, curious and led by her heart and who takes matters into her own hands, so the impact of the Suffragettes on her character development seems like a natural fit. 

How has it been working with Arielle Smith and Aaron S. Watkin, during this production? As a performer, have you taken anything away from this collaboration that you’ll continue to do in your next roles?

I love the rehearsal time on a role as I feel that is when you discover the most and can really push yourself to explore new ideas that will help the audience to forget they are watching choreography and just become enraptured in the story. I have been working on achieving this in the studio with Aaron and I’m really grateful for his coaching, particularly in the main pas de deux with Clara and the Prince. Working with Arielle, especially on Clara’s entrance in Act 1, I was able to really understand where she took some of her inspiration from in the creation of this scene. I took a lot of inspiration from her directly as to who Clara’s character is, being able to understand what drove each of her decisions in the choreography gives Clara the intention that really defines her. 

As a performer, what is your earliest memory of the Nutcracker?

I grew up obsessively watching Barbie in the Nutcracker with my sisters (and Dad, who secretly loved them…). When performing as Clara now, I really want to be able to give the younger audience the same feeling that I had as a child watching this movie…the iconic music, the idea of magic, falling in love for the first time, the whimsical story, and giving me my love for ballet.  

Is there a standout moment of Nutcracker that you’re particularly excited to perform?

I think I’m mostly just excited to be taken on Clara’s journey and be able to perform such beautiful pas de deux’s to the most iconic live music played by the English National Ballet Philharmonic. 


Why do you think people should come and see the Nutcracker at the London Coliseum?

It's a beautiful family tradition for everyone to enjoy. Nutcracker really has something in it for everyone. There are so many fun characters to be introduced to along the way, a magical storyline, incredible live music, the most whimsical sets and costumes, and many surprises along the way.  

How is this performance different from others that have been put on in the past?

It’s such an uplifting, imaginative, colourful show that transports you on a magical journey from the moment the overture begins…

English National Ballet’s production of The Nutcracker plays at the London Coliseum from 17 December to 10 January 2027.

item.title: Eurotrash at The Young Vic Review
item.dc:creator: Penny Walshe
item.description:
Based on the 2025 Booker Prize-nominated autobiographical story, Colin Teevan adapts Christian Kracht’s Eurotrash for the stage at the Young Vic. Starring Ben Whishaw (Black Doves) and Kathryn Hunter (Ann Droid), Walter Meierjohann directs an ambitious, large-scale production that intricately explores past trauma and class guilt through a complex mother-son relationship.

The story follows blocked writer Christian (Whishaw), who pays his 80-year-old mother (Hunter) a visit at a psychiatric ward in Zurich. Despite the mother’s age and alcoholism, they embark on a spontaneous journey across Switzerland with the aim of giving away her fortune in hard cash. Packed with outlandish humour, their chaotic road trip is somewhat of a fever dream, searching for connection and atonement.

One of the key themes in Eurotrash is Vergangenheitsbewältigung, a German term for "coming to terms with history" that is commonly used when referring to the atrocities committed during World War II. The mother often refers to their position as a "class disease", alluding to their dark family history and the role of her Nazi-supporting father. Their journey feels cathartic for them both as they attempt to escape the memories that haunt them.

Whishaw and Hunter’s chemistry is excellent. Hunter’s cutting, larger-than-life drunk mother is balanced by Whishaw’s reluctant caregiver role. The love and resentment between them create an infectious energy and aid the storytelling perfectly. Their starkly different characters generate many funny moments through absurdity and slapstick. There are also moments amidst their bickering when their relationship harmonises and they become emotionally vulnerable with one another. These rare moments offer effective poignancy within a fast-paced narrative.

The staging is a technical masterpiece. Lizzie Clachan’s set, which acts as arguably the play’s main character, is bold and rich in symbolism. Set within a clinical white airport lounge against the stunning backdrop of the Swiss mountains, the space is manipulated in numerous ways to create different locations throughout their journey. The title Eurotrash is also taken very literally in the stage design. Above the windows overlooking the mountains lies a travelator, with designer bags and souvenirs continuously moving across it before falling into a recycling bin at the end. This is just one example of how Clachan explores class guilt through the set, where every square metre of the stage can be interpreted through the play’s central themes.

Proving to be one of the most ambitious productions of 2026, Eurotrash is undeniably an exceptional staging, though its ambition occasionally overreaches at the expense of the plot.

Meierjohann’s entertaining 1hr 45min dramedy is performing at the Young Vic until 9 January 2027.

★★★★

Written by Becky for Theatre and Tonic, November 2026.

item.title: Desire Under The Elms at Almeida Theatre Review
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Bywater
item.description:
Eugene O’Neill was one of the architects of twentieth-century American drama, revolutionising theatre with his shift towards psychological realism. His lesser-known play Desire Under The Elms was banned in the UK for sixteen years for its depiction of incest, adultery, and infanticide. Now, former Almeida Resident Director Ebenezer Bamgboye revitalises its taboo elements by transplanting it to the Deep South in the early 1900s in a production which is seismically visceral but equally enervating.

Bamgboye extracts the play’s Greek tragic framework by installing a trio of musical spirits who puppeteer the characters and their movements, led by a magnetic Choolwe Laina Muntanga who opens with a rendition of ‘House of the Rising Sun’. He also sharpens the play’s concerns with greed and desire by interweaving a racial element, making Eben the sole black family member. A bitter war with his father Ephraim over the deed to the family’s hardscrabble farm and an obsessive sexual relationship with his new stepmother Abbie are heightened by an unspoken societal conflict. 

Zackary Momoh delivers a charged Eben, whose obsessive pacing across Basia Bińkowska’s sandstone set eventually manifests into gnarled, jerky movements of anger as he battles with obsession and desire. He is equally vulnerable, offering a portrayal that trickles with fatigue and repression. His desire to honour his late mother, whom Ephraim worked to death, takes on a new weight when he confronts his father as a quasi-slavemaster. 

Antony Byrne is exacting as the volatile patriarch who is cootish in measure; violent outbursts are paired with optimistic chatter, conveying a man whose own greed has emotionally stunted him. It is, however, Kelly Gough’s mesmerising turn as his new bride which radiates throughout the piece. Her dexterous, visceral portrayal climaxes when her obsessive desire for Eben swallows her, unleashing ungodly cries as grotesque as the blood she smears in the play’s final moments. 

Bamboye does a great deal in stretching the confines of the text, particularly through his collaboration with movement and intimacy director Rose Ryan whose slow-motion vignettes, placed in key moments of tension between Eben and Abbie, accentuate their carnal movements. But, it is often a noisy, overstated production — particularly in the first act when Bamboye’s stylistic intentions shroud the detailed edges of O’Neill’s plot. Incessant on-stage pacing, hollow motifs such as a bucket of water that looms over the action until the end, and bursts of lighting from the back of the set all begin to compete with one another in a play that already has enough going on.

It’s a galvanised take on an oft-forgotten American classic, but don’t expect energy without exhaustion.

Desire Under The Elms runs until 23 December at Almeida Theatre, London.

★★★

 Written by David for Theatre and Tonic, November 2026.

item.title: A Homo Alone 2 at The Other Palace Studio Review
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Bywater
item.description:
Queer festive chaos at its finest! A Homo Alone 2 at the Other Palace, written by Jodie Prenger and Neil Hurst and directed by Laura Checkley, is the perfect Christmas night out. Packed with brilliant musical numbers, show stealing performances and non-stop laughter. Following the success of their previous Christmas parodies including Lovers Actually and Homo Alone, this production has been commissioned by the Other Palace to kick Christmas off with a bang.

I’m sure many of you are familiar with the plot of Home Alone 2, we follow the young Kevin McAllister lost and alone in New York while his family are on a different flight to their vacation in Florida. This show kept everything we love about the film, with a large sprinkling of silliness added on top. Kevin, played by Thomas John Stocks, instead of being a young boy is now a twink finally free to do whatever – or whoever – he wants in the city. Stocks brought a wonderful energy to the stage and was the perfect naïve protagonist to follow through this night of fun and laughter. Jenny Bede and Charlotte Dixon’s impressive multi-rolling brought joy and pace to the production, while both having incredible singing voices, they held on to the aesthetic of the original film with Dixon’s wonderfully hunched over and scheming Marv driving the story and Bede’s over the top Catherine O’Hara impression never letting us down as Kevin’s not so concerned mother. All the performers had the audience in the palm of their hands, barely giving us time to breathe in between each moment of hilarity.  

However, one performer in particular stole the show for me. Jermaine Woods multi-rolling as Kevin’s closeted dad, to the mischievous criminal Harry, to a full-blown Rocky Horror performance as Tim Curry were some of the most brilliant and energetic character performances I have seen in a long time. Each time Woods came on stage I couldn’t wait to see what happened next and his comedic timing landed every joke. This cast lit up the stage and created an unforgettable musical evening.

The audience participation really brought the whole theatre into the show. With actors passing props to audience members, having the front row re-enact the famous “Kevin’s not here” bag pass and even getting us to throw pigeons at the criminals. With individual audience members getting picked on over and over again and often being the butt of the joke, it truly felt like we were having a unique experience at this show and the production succeeded in bringing the audience together to take part in the joy on stage.

A Homo Alone 2 was a kinky and hilarious Christmas night out that I would recommend to any group of friends this festive season.

Playing at the Other Palace Studio from the 18th of November to the 3rd of January 2027.  

★★★★

 Written by George for Theatre and Tonic, November 2026.
